full_judgment:
26. The learned Advocate for the petitioner refereed to a Hydarabad decision in the case of Shawkat-un-nessa Vs. The State of Hydarabad, reported in AIR 1950 Hydarabad at page 20 in which a criminal proceeding instituted against Mir Laik Ali & others were quashed, instituted for reasons of his illegal escape from house detention. That decision is not relevant in the facts of the instant case as in that case Mir Laik Ali and others were put on home detention under the Hydarabad Regulation which Regulation after the coming into force of the Constitution of India in January 1950 was declared void by the Supreme Court being inconsistent with the fundamental rights and it was held that the said law under which Mir Laik Ali and others were detained being declared void, Laik Ali and others cannot be said to be in legal detention and for his escape no criminal proceeding would lie. and hence the said was quashed which fact is different from the case in hand because in the instant case the detention order was under section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act and it had never been declared void yet. That case thus, we do not find to be of much relevance in the instant case except to the extent that a detention law under which a detention order is passed if declared void, the detention order would have no legs to stand and the law empowering the detaining authority to pass the order having been found to be void there would be no detention order legally existing at the time a person in yet in the detention but nothing further. We have seen that the learned Judges of the Full Bench of that court delivering separate judgments though agreeing with each other, had been anxious to find whether at the time of detention and before it was declared void or during the detention period any criminal offence had been committed by Laik Ali and they found no such criminal act or criminal offence committed or criminal liability incurred separately from the detention order. 

 45. Now the question arises as to whether the decision of the High Court Division declaring the detention of the detenu illegal will be treated as prospective taking effect from the date when the court passed the order, or it will have retrospective effect from the date of the initial order of detention passed by the detaining authority, Mr. Hossain submits that the petitioner was not under any obligation to comply with the order of detaining authority found invalid by the Superior Court in view of the fact that the said order of the court has taken its effect from the date of the initial order and has rendered all the subsequent orders arising out of the original order of detention as invalid and the present proceeding having arisen during the subsistence of the order of detention later on declared invalid, is liable to be quashed to prevent the abuse of the process of the court and to avoid unnecessary harassment of the petitioner who has committed no offence under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act. A few decisions have been cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner to show that for disobeying an illegal order one can not be held liable to be prosecuted. It is needless to mention the case referred to as the subject matter of those cases are different and distinguishable having no relevancy with the instant case. The principle laid down in the case of Shawkat-un-nessa Vs, The State reported in AIR (37) 1950 Hydarabad (FB) 20 cited by learned Advocate for the petitioner though comes near to the point does not exactly support the contention of the petitioner, the facts and circumstances of the two case being different. The fact of the cited case is that Mr. Laik Ali, the erstwhile Prime Minister of Hydarabad while detained under the Hydarabad Regulation escaped from the custody and a Criminal Proceeding was initiated against him and the other persons who were alleged to have helped him in making good his escape. The Full Bench of Hydarabad High Court held that the detention order being ex facie void and the Constitution of India when Hydarabad became part of India, Mir Laik Ali and for that matter his associates committed no offence. In the said case all the Judges of the Full Bench of Hydarabad High Court including Nail CJ in their respective judgment delivered separately were in agreement on the point that Mir Laik Ali being not held under any lawful custody or lawful detention, his escape from such detention did not constitute any Criminal Offence. In the instant case the petitioner was not taken to be held in custody by way of securing his arrest in pursuance of the first order of detention and the petitioner having not complied with the order of the detaining authority is alleged to have committed offence under section 7(b) of the Special Powers Act and, therefore, the principles laid down in the above cited case have no manner of application in the present case.
